title: Apricot Finance - TTFT playbook & self-serve onramp discovery

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-25
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Jordan Miles (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Evan Cho (Redwood SE); Samir Patel (CTO), Leah Ong (Lead ML Eng), Marco Ruiz (Security), Dina Kaur (PM)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we appreciate you taking the time. Quick intro — I'm Jordan, AE at Redwood Inference, with Priya and Evan from our SE team. How's everyone doing?
[00:12] Samir: Good, thanks. Busy week but excited to get through this — we want to understand how fast we can go from PoC to API first call, basically TTFT, and what the security constraints look like.
[00:24] Jordan: Perfect, that's the plan of this call. We'll run through the self-serve flow, free credit runway, and then surf into hosted vs dedicated vs private options, and finish with next steps.
[00:35] Priya: Quick note: when we say "TTFT" we mean from account creation to first successful generate or embed API call that mirrors your payload size and concurrency.
[00:45] Leah: Yeah — for us payloads are 800-1,200 tokens per request, typical batch sizes small, plus we'll likely need streaming for real-time scoring.
[00:56] Jordan: Good data point. That token size influences kernel selection and latency.
[01:05] Evan: Also curious about prefix/K V cache behavior — if you have repeated contexts across requests we can show caching improvements. Sometimes the auto caching is called "KV cache" in docs but it's spelled out weirdly in transcripts.
[01:18] Marco: Before we dive too deep, security first: we need to know whether hosted means any PII leaves their VPC, how keys are managed, and can we control encryption keys (KMS/HSM)? Also audit logs and SSO/SAML.
[01:32] Jordan: Totally. For self-serve hosted API, data is encrypted in transit and at rest, and we offer customer-managed keys via KMS integrations in Redwood Private. We'll send a detailed security pack after the call. Briefly: hosted has tenancy isolation but not VPC peering; Dedicated gives reserved capacity and predictable throughput; Private gives full VPC/on-prem options and your KMS.
[01:50] Samir: Ok, but for our compliance we likely need private or dedicated? We're a regulated fintech. We can't have raw transaction PII go outside.
[01:58] Priya: Understood. Often teams start with a hosted evaluation using synthetic or anonymized inputs — that's the fastest TTFT — then move to dedicated or private for production.
[02:10] Dina: What's the typical TTFT you've seen for engineering teams here? Two hours? A day?
[02:16] Jordan: Good question. For a basic self-serve with typical webhooks and a straightforward prompt, many teams are hitting first successful calls under 30 minutes. A slightly more realistic setup with SDKs, auth, and sample payloads tends to be 1-2 hours. For regulated pilots where you need VPC/dedicated, provisioning takes days to weeks depending on contract.
[02:39] Leah: That 30 minutes is promising. We want to validate latency under our traffic shape though — 800-1,200 tokens, p50/p95.
[02:47] Evan: We can provide a quick benchmark harness you can run locally against the hosted endpoint — we'll include sample payloads and a runbook to collect p50/p95 and cost per 1k tokens.
[02:58] Jordan: And we'll give you 2,000 free inference credits to run that smoke/baseline test; it's enough to simulate a few hundred calls at your token sizes.
[03:07] Samir: Nice — that helps. How do those credits map to token math?
[03:11] Jordan: We'll include a breakdown: tokens per request * number of requests. Essentially credits -> token units, we'll attach a small spreadsheet.
[03:20] Marco: Another security nit: retention — do logs with request/response persist? For PCI-ish contexts we need ephemeral retention or log redaction.
[03:30] Priya: Hosted default retention is 30 days for request traces but you can opt into retention reductions, and in Private you control retention entirely. We'll include retention policy bullets in the security pack.
[03:42] Leah: Great. On the technical stack — we use Kubernetes on AWS, some on-prem for sensitive workloads. We'd prefer API compatibility so we can abstract server calls later. How much code change is needed to switch between hosted and private?
[03:56] Jordan: Very little — same REST/SDK interface across modes. The main changes are auth endpoint and trunking to VPC or private endpoint. We try to keep the surface area stable so your code paths don't need rework.
[04:09] Dina: Do you support function/tool calling or streaming in self-serve?
[04:14] Priya: Yes, streaming responses and function-like structured output are available in hosted API; we'll show a short demo link in the quickstart.
[04:22] Samir: Can we see a sample quickstart for a credit-card transaction classification flow? Even pseudo code.
[04:28] Evan: We have a sample repo with a fraud classification example — we can adapt it to your payloads. We'll send that link and a small snippet to add to your CI smoke harness.
[04:38] Leah: On model selection — do you provide profiles for model latency and cost? We might trade quality vs cost for scoring.
[04:45] Jordan: Yes. We maintain a model catalog with performance profiles. Redwood Optimize gives guidance on quantization or smaller variants for scoring workloads. For prototype, we'd recommend starting with a verified open model that's cost-efficient, and we can show the perf vs cost curve.
[04:58] Marco: Any concerns about hallucinations for classification tasks? Our outputs must be deterministic-ish.
[05:04] Priya: For classification and reranking, we tune decoding settings, temperature to 0 in many cases, and use structured outputs + eval harness to catch regressions. We'll recommend a prompt template and an eval set you can run.
[05:16] Samir: Ok that's helpful. Walk me through the exact steps we should do this week to hit TTFT.
[05:22] Jordan: Step 1: we'll email you a one-click quickstart that creates a free account and pre-loads sample keys and a tiny repo. Step 2: drop in your sample anonymized payloads and run the included benchmark harness. Step 3: collect p50/p95 and send results back; we'll help interpret.
[05:36] Samir: How fast will we see kernels and batching effects? Our tokens are long, does continuous batching help?
[05:44] Evan: Batching helps throughput and cost, but if you're latency-sensitive, we can tune to smaller batch thresholds. Our runtime supports dynamic batching and will pick kernels based on seq length distribution. For long sequences, the per-token cost is higher, but caching repeated prefixes reduces cost if applicable.
[05:58] Leah: Is there a sandbox to run streaming behavior?
[06:01] Priya: Yes — the quickstart includes a streaming sample that shows progressive tokens and chunk sizes.
[06:09] Dina: On billing and cost controls — can we cap spend during the self-serve trial?
[06:14] Jordan: You get free credits by default for the pilot. Beyond that, you can set quotas and soft/hard limits in the console; we'll walk you through recommended limits.
[06:25] Marco: For compliance audit logs — is there a way to get an export?
[06:29] Priya: Yes, logs can be exported to S3 or delivered to your SIEM in dedicated/private modes. In hosted mode we provide an export API for audit traces.
[06:40] Samir: About private deployment — we have some on-prem clusters behind a firewall. How involved is the private on-prem install?
[06:47] Evan: On-prem has an installation runbook; typical lead time is 4-8 weeks for full on-prem with HSM integration, depending on procurement. We often recommend starting hosted for experiments then moving to private for compliance.
[06:59] Leah: That aligns with our internal plan. We'll try hosted with redacted payloads and then plan a dedicated/private pilot once we have baseline metrics.
[07:07] Jordan: Excellent. We'll provision the 2k credits and send the quickstart link and the security pack right after.
[07:12] Dina: One more practical Q: do you have SDKs in Python and Java?
[07:16] Priya: Yes — Python, Node, Java, and a curl example. We'll attach snippets.
[07:22] Samir: On the benchmarking harness — can you include a small test that simulates concurrency of 20 rps with a mixing distribution?
[07:28] Evan: Yes, we can provide a Locust/JMeter template and a lightweight runner script. We'll put the concurrency patterns in the runbook.
[07:36] Jordan: Quick objection handling: You'll hear from procurement about longer SLA windows and data residency guarantees — that's normal. For most adoption paths, the sequence is pilot (hosted) -> dedicated (reserved capacity) -> private for regulated workloads.
[07:49] Marco: Any customers in fintech who did followed that path?
[07:52] Jordan: Yes, a handful — we'll include anonymized case notes.
[07:56] Leah: Are there any gotchas with prompt templatization and escaping for JSON payloads?
[08:02] Priya: Sometimes double encoding happens. We'll include template patterns and a helper lib in the quickstart to safely inject JSON fields.
[08:10] Samir: OK let's recap what you will send.
[08:13] Jordan: We'll send: quickstart link + pre-provisioned 2,000 credits, security pack (SOC2, retention, KMS notes), sample fraud-classification repo, benchmark harness with concurrency templates, and a short invite for a 30-min result review.
[08:27] Dina: That works. We'll aim to run the smoke test by Thursday and share results.
[08:31] Jordan: Great. Any other questions?
[08:34] Marco: Nothing else from security for now but we'll follow up after reading the pack.
[08:39] Leah: No, that's it — thanks.
[08:41] Jordan: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up within 24 hours.

--- end of recorded portion (auto timestamps are approximate)

Notes about transcription: some proper nouns and acronyms may be mis-transcribed (eg: KV cache as K V cache), filler words and interruptions present. The call had moderate crosstalk during Q&A.
